8 |   P a g e  1.2.   Research Gap  Existing child safety wearables focus on location tracking and manual SOS activation. They lack proactive detection of acoustic distress and do not personalize alerts to the child’s trusted caregivers. Many cloud-based audio monitoring solutions upload raw audio, posing privacy risks and introducing latency and connectivity dependencies [1]. Furthermore, children’s play naturally involves shouting and laughter; therefore, a naive screaming detector would generate frequent false alarms. No commercial product currently combines distress detection, speaker verification, contextual information, and on-device learning into a single wearable component. The research gap lies in designing a tiny dual-model pipeline that runs entirely on the watch, adapts to the child’s normal environment, utilizes context cues to reduce false positives, and preserves privacy by keeping raw audio on the device. 9 |   P a g e  1.3.   Research Problem  Design a stranger-threat detection component for children's wearables that (a) makes real-time predictions of likelihood of acoustic distress, (b) verifies that speech is from registered trusted voices through the device, (c) combine these likelihoods with contextual clues (geofence and parent device distance) to compute a risk score, (d) adapt thresholds and trusted voices through on-device learning, and (e) operates under hard latency (<50 ms per frame), power (<10 % dayper-day battery), and false alarm (<5 %) limits. The system should operate without uploading raw audio off the watch and should provide minimal metadata to guardians to preserve privacy  2.   OBJECTIVES  2.1   Main Objective  To build, deploy, and evaluate a privacy-friendly voice-based stranger threat detection for kid wear that actively detects distress incidents, verifies trusted voices, and applies context to deliver credible alerts while maintaining on-device privacy  2.2   Specific Objectives  •   Collecting and Curating the Dataset: Assemble a balanced dataset from publicly available emotional/distress databases (Women & Children Danger, Audio Set “Screaming”, RAVDESS, CREMA-D, SAVEE, TESS), environmental sounds datasets (UrbanSound8K, ESC-50,  FSD50K), and a restricted, consenting watch-microphone dataset. Prepare all audio into mono 16 kHz, 1-s windows with 50 % overlap and compute log-Mel spectrograms.  •   Global Danger Sound Model: Design a light-weight model from MobileNetV2/V3 that has <1 M parameters. Fine-tune using class-balanced loss functions, data augmentations, and watchquality data-based fine-tuning. Prune the model and apply quantization-aware training to generate an 8-bit TFLite model that has less than a 50 ms per-frame inference time.  •   Personal Circle of Trust Model: Integrate a speaker verification system using Resemblyzer or Speech Brain ECAPA-TDNN embeddings. Develop a voice enrollment procedure for caregivers and translate cosine similarity into P(trusted voice) using calibrated sigmoid functions. Keep embeddings safely stored on the device using Android Keystore or iOS Keychain.  •   Risk Smoothing and Fusion: Define the risk calculation Risk = wd · P(distress) · (1 −

Include context nudges based on geofencing and BLE proximity to adjust the alert threshold.  •   On-Device Adaptation: Develop clustering methods (Mini Batch K-Means or DBSCAN) that detect long-lived unknown voices and alert parents to add new trusted speakers. Maintain online statistics of environmental energy noises to adapt thresholds to typical play.  •   Implementation and Integration: Build an end-to-end pipeline in WearOS. Gate the pipeline with Voice Activity Detection (WebRTC/Silero), run models with TFLite and the XNNPACK delegate, and interleave Android Location and BLE APIs for context. Measure computation and power usage with Android Studio Power Profiler.  •   Evaluation: Establish quantitative specifications (recall >90 %, FAR <5 %, latency ≤2 s, battery impact <10 %) and conduct experiments through controlled datasets and field trials. Get guardian feedback for usability and nuisance alarm.  •   Deliverables: Make a working wearable device prototype, a smartphone sidekick app, an evaluation report, and deliverable-ready documentation for potential future deployment or commercialization.

11 |   P a g e  3.   METHODOLOGY  3.1   Datasets and Data Collection  To train robust models, the project will combine multiple open datasets (Table 1.1) along with a bespoke watch-microphone dataset recorded under consent.  Dataset Name   Classes / Content   Clips / Duration   Purpose   Citation  Women &  Children in Danger  Child danger, woman danger, normal  19,375   Distress examples   [4]  Audio Set “Screaming”  Screaming, other   1000   Distress examples   [9]  UrbanSound8K   10 (e.g., kids playing, siren)  8732   Normal backgrounds  [5]  ESC-50   50 (e.g., animal, home sounds)  2000   Normal backgrounds  [6]  FSD50K   200 sound types   7356   Angry/scary talk   [8]  SAVEE   7 emotions   480   Emotion training   [10]  TESS   7 emotions   2800   Emotion training   [11]  Watch Mic Data   Distress, normal play  500   Device tuning   N/A  Table 1.2 : Dataset Summary  All datasets shall be resampled into mono at a rate of 16 kHz, windowed into segments of 1 s width with 50 % overlap, and normalized. Positive examples of distress shall be screams, crying, speech during anger, and fearful faces; negative examples shall be ordinary environmental sounds and natural speech. The consent watch dataset shall be collected after getting ethical clearance and shall comprise sentences spoken by caregivers and children playing for fine-tuning the models for the target device's acoustics.

12 |   P a g e  3.2 Feature Extraction and Pre-Processing  All windows of the audio will be converted into a log-Mel spectrogram in 32–64 Mel bands.  The signal is windowed (e.g., windows of 25 ms at a hop of 10 ms), the Short-Time Fourier Transform is computed and mapped into the Mel scale; the magnitude is also transformed into decibels by a logarithmic calculation. The output time–frequency “image” preserves pitch and temporal structure and is available for CNN input. Ablation experiments may computationally calculate Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs).  To introduce a higher level of robustness, we will use common augmentations: additive noise from MUSAN (speech/music/noise), randomness in gain, time stretching, pitch shifting, and time–frequency masks (Spec Augment). They will be parameterized not to alter label semantics and introduce realistic distortions. All pre-processing will be coded in Python using librosa and plugged into TensorFlow data pipelines for efficient learning.  3.3   Global Danger Sound Model  The Global Danger Sound Model estimates the probability that a given 1-s window has distress. It will be trained using MobileNet-V2 or Small MobileNet-V3 backbones, employing inverted residual blocks and depth-wise separable convolutions due to their efficiency. These have proven effective for on-device audio classification (e.g., YAMNet employs a MobileNet V1 [2]). A width multiplier from 0.35 to 0.75 will control parameter count ( ＜ 1 M). The input size (e.g., 64×96) is 64 Mel bands by 96 time frames.  Loss and Training: Because events of worry are rarer than negatives, a focal loss (γ = 2) or class-weighted cross-entropy loss will minimize class imbalance. Training will be done twice: pre-training over the big publicly available datasets, and fine-tuning over the consent watch dataset through k-fold cross-validation. Early stopping based on the validation false alarm rate will prevent overfitting. Augmented data will foster diversity.  Model Compression: To meet the watch’s energy and memory constraints, we will apply pruning and quantization-aware training (QAT). Pruning zeros out near-zero weights and retains sparse matrices that can be sparsely represented; QAT compacts weights and activations into 8-bit integers at the expense of very minimal loss in accuracy. The compressed TFLite model (~500 kB) will be validated through the official benchmark.

13 |   P a g e  3.4 Personal “Circle of Trust” Model  Speaker verification confirms that the system differentiates between well-known caregivers and unknown voices. At enrollment, each caregiver speaks 3–5 statements (5–10 s). Audio passes through a speaker encoder and produces embedding; Resemblyzer provides 256dimensional embeddings and makes it easy for developers to represent segments of audio as vectors [3]. Alternatively, use the Speech Brain ECAPATDNN model (192-D). A centroid (mean vector) is computed for each speaker. At inference, after detection of voice activity, the system computes the last speech segment's embedding and computes cosine similarity for each enrolled centroid; maximum similarity is converted into P(trusted) by a calibrated sigmoid. If no speech is detected (silence), P(trusted) = 1 so that no penalty is assigned for silence.  Storage and Security: We maintain only embeddings and centroids locally on the device and store them securely through the Android Keystore or Keychain for iOS. We save no raw audio. Enrollment operations require parent authentication. Voice Activity Detection (VAD): A light-weight VAD module (e.g., WebRTC GMM-based or Silero NN-based) gates the speaker verification chain so that it does not compute embeddings when there is no speech at all. This ensures that the trust model is only triggered when there is speech.

14 |   P a g e  3.5 Risk Fusion and Smoothing  For each audio window, the watch computes:  Risk   =   w d   ·   P (distress) · (1 −   P (trusted))+   δ unknown ,  where   w d   is a weight (initially 1.0) and   δ unknown   is a small penalty (e.g., 0.05–0.15) applied when speech is detected but not recognized as trusted. The instantaneous risk values are processed through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with smoothing factor   α   ≈ 0 . 3 to avoid flickering alerts. A dynamic threshold   T   is set (e.g., 0.85) and modified by context:  •   Geofence: If the child is inside trusted areas (home or school), the threshold increases slightly (∆   >   0). Outside safe zones, the threshold decreases (−∆) to favor detection.  •   Parent BLE proximity: The presence of a paired parent device via BLE nudges the threshold upwards ( δ >   0). Absence nudges it downwards (− δ ).  An alert is triggered only when the smoothed risk exceeds the threshold for a dwell time (e.g., 1–2 s). The alert payload includes the event label, risk confidence, and coarse location; no audio is transmitted.  Figure 1.1: Risk Fusion and Thresholding  3.6   On-Device Learning and Adaptation

15 |   P a g e  The system continuously adjusts by learning from its world without transferring audio. Trusted Voice Expansion:   Repeatedly observed embeddings of unknown speakers that appear around the child are grouped by Minibatch K-Means or DBSCAN. If the cluster is observed over more than one session, the parent is asked for permission to move the voice into the trusted list.  Once approved, a few embeddings are collected and the centroid is saved securely.   Baseline Adaptation:   To reduce false alarms during normal play, streaming statistics (e.g., energy and spectral centroid) are tracked using exponential smoothing or streaming quantile estimators. If the current audio is like the baseline profile, the risk score decreases slightly. These adjustments are conservative, not to suppress the real threat.  Figure 1.2: Post-Deployment Learning Workflow

16 |   P a g e  3.7   System Implementation Plan  Figure 1.3: High-Level System Architecture  •   Audio Capture:   Continuous recording from the watch mic into a ring buffer. We process in 1-second frames at a 0.5-second hop.  •   Voice Activity Detection:   A tiny VAD module checks for speech or a loud event in frame. If not, it sleeps.  •   Feature Extraction:   Log-Mel spectrogram computation runs locally on device using optimized C++/TFLite.  •   Global Danger Model:   The compacted MobileNet model forecasts   P(distress) .  •   Speaker Verification:   If there is speech, the trust model computes embeddings and compares them to trusted centroids to generate   P(trusted) .  •   Risk Fusion:   Combines probabilities, applies an unknown voice penalty and contextbased nudges (like geofence & BLE), then smooths the result over time.

17 |   P a g e  •   Alert Manager:   When risk stays above the threshold for a set duration, it sends an alert via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi to the guardian’s phone. The app displays the alert and optional map location.  •   On-Device Learning:   Maintains embedding buffers and baseline statistics, triggers prompts for adding new trusted voices, and adapts thresholds as needed.  Implementation Tools:  •   Software:  TensorFlow/Keras for model development  TensorFlow Lite with XNNPACK delegate for on-device inference  WebRTC VAD or Silero VAD  Android APIs for audio, geofencing, and BLE scanning PyTorch or Speech Brain for alternative speaker encoders scikit-learn for clustering  •   Hardware:  Wear OS smartwatches (e.g., Snapdragon Wear 4100 or newer)  Android smartphone for the   parent device  GPU-enabled development workstation for training and experimentation  3.8   Handling Offline Scenarios and Connectivity Issues.  The solution is tolerant of infrequent internet connections. While offline, all important threat alerts are stored locally on the smartwatch. The alert is time-stamped and queued to be sent to the backend server as soon as the device gets back online to ensure that no alert is lost. To enable a timely response in offline scenarios, the device has a local, attentionseeking audio alarm that can alert individuals in close proximity.

18 |   P a g e  4.   PROJECT REQUIREMENTS  4.1 Functional Requirements (FR)  FR-1: Recording in-device and Voice-Activated Device  Capture permanently mono 16 kHz audio from the watch. Use a light-weight VAD (“speech / loud event”) gate to decide when downstream models should run in order to maintain power.  FR-2: Global Threat Tone Model  Run a tiny CNN (e.g., MobileNet-V2/V3-Small TFLite int8) on log-Mel features to estimate P(distress) ∈ [0,1] for 1 s windows (50% overlap).  FR-3: One "Circle of Trust" (speaker verification)  When speech is detected by VAD, compute an on-device embedding and estimate P(trusted voice) ∈ [0,1] by cosine-similarity to enrolled caregivers (no raw audio is retained).  FR-4: Risk fusion & smoothing  Compute per-window Risk = wd   ⋅   P(distress) ⋅ (1−P(trusted))+δ unknown. Apply EMA smoothing (α≈0.3, 2–3 s). Trigger alerts only if EMA(Risk) > dynamic threshold T′ for dwell 1–  2 s.  FR-5: Location/geofencing context  Maintain trusted geofences (e.g., Home, School; radius ≥100 m; use DWELL). Inside safe zones:  T′=T+Δ (Δ≈+0.05…+0.08). Outside: T′=T−Δ (Δ≈0.03…0.06). Store only coarse place labels in alerts.  FR-6: BLE parent-device proximity  Conduct brief scan spurts using Bluetooth LE Scanner filters (parent MAC/UUID). If parent is present (RSSI ≥ −70 dBm observed ≤60 s): T′=T + δ (δ≈+0.02…+0.05). If not present ≥3  FR-7: Alerts & guardian app

19 |   P a g e  Send alerts only in metadata (label, confidence, timestamp, coarse location, parent-near flag).  Supply acknowledge/snooze on the guardian device. No audio leaves the watch.  FR-8: Privacy & security  Store only embeddings, centroids, and light-weight statistics. Encrypt at rest (Keystore/Keychain). Authenticate enrollment/management operations.  FR-9: Enrollment & configuration  Allow caregiver registration (3–5 concise statements), geofencing setup, parent-device synchronization, and parameters for safe tuning (T, Δ, δ, dwell).  FR-10: On-device learning  (a)   Expansion of trusted-voice: cluster repeat unknown embeddings; with parental permission, introduce as trusted.  (b)   Modality adaptation of baseline: store EMA of energy/bands to slightly de-weight risk during normal play (never to zero).  FR-11: Diagnostics (metadata only)  Keep rotating, on-device metadata logs for debugging (no audio): timestamps, decisions, model latency, battery usage, flags for context.  FR-12: Safety bias guard-rails  If there are two consecutive windows and P(distress)≥0.95 or hard-event rule holds (e.g., sharp scream), skip nudges and alarm immediately.

20 |   P a g e  4.2 Non-Functional Requirements (NFR)  NFR-1(Latency):  Inference should take less than 50 milliseconds per 1-second audio window on the target watch, and complete alert delivery must stay under 2 seconds end-to-end.  NFR-2 (Battery):  The system should consume less than 10% of the battery per day under typical usage (including VAD always on, occasional Bluetooth scans, and location updates during geofence changes).  NFR-3 (Model Footprint):  The global model must stay under 1 million parameters, with its TFLite int8 version taking up no more than ~500 KB. It should also comfortably run within the memory limits of the watch.  NFR-4 (Precision):  In field testing, the system should identify at least 90% of distress cases (recall), while keeping false alarms (false alarm rate) below 5%.  NFR-5 (Robustness):  The system should handle everyday background noise (like sirens, playgrounds, traffic) and multiple languages effectively. If certain sensors or permissions are unavailable, it should continue to function gracefully.  NFR-6 (Security):  Use hardware-backed encryption keys when available, and enforce role-based access control for tasks like enrolling caregivers or managing settings.  NFR-7 (Privacy):  Never store or transmit raw audio. Keep telemetry to a minimum and follow consent workflows for parental control.  NFR-8 (Usability):  Allow easy setup with single-tap prompts. Alerts should be clearly presented with a user-friendly design and should not interrupt unnecessarily.

21 |   P a g e  NFR-9 (Accessibility):  Interface should support high-contrast visuals, readable fonts, and include haptic (vibration) feedback for important interactions.  NFR-10 (Portability):  Design should work on Wear OS and be easily transferable to watchOS using Core ML, with no need for architectural changes.  NFR-11 (Maintainability):  Build the system in a modular way (e.g., VAD, models, fusion logic, and context modules), with configurable options and support for over-the-air (OTA) updates for both models and configurations.  NFR-12 (Scalability):  If a cloud backend is used for configuration or telemetry, it must scale to support a growing number of devices while ensuring only limited metadata (no audio) is uploaded at controlled rates.  NFR-13 (Ethics/Compliance):  Document consent processes clearly. Ensure minimal data collection, and design the experience with child safety in mind, following all relevant privacy laws and regulations.  4.3 Expected Test Cases  TC-01 – VAD Gate Function:  Goal: Make sure the system only computes when the VAD detects sound.  Setup: Background noise with a VAD threshold set.  Steps: Play silence → normal speech → loud non-speech.  Expected Outcome: Models should only activate for actual speech or loud events.  Pass Criteria: At least 90% of silent windows should not trigger model inference.  TC-02 – Distress Detection (Screams/Crying):  Goal: Confirm system picks up real distress.  Setup: Use labeled clips from both lab and field.

22 |   P a g e  Steps: Stream distress sounds into the device.  Expected Outcome: Risk score crosses threshold (T) and triggers alerts.  Pass Criteria: ≥90% recall; latency ≤2 seconds.  TC-03 – False Alarms in Safe Geofence:  Goal: Avoid false alarms in “safe” zones.  Setup: Inside “Home” with DWELL; simulate playful loudness. Steps: Kids playing loudly.  Expected Outcome: System keeps risk below adjusted threshold T' = T + Δ.  Pass Criteria: ≥50% fewer nuisance alerts compared to no-context baseline.  TC-04 – Sensitivity Outside Geofence:  Goal: Increase alert sensitivity when outside safe zones.  Setup: Not in any geofenced area.  Steps: Play borderline distress sounds.  Expected Outcome: Lower threshold T' = T - Δ triggers alert.  Pass Criteria: Recall at least as good as baseline; FAR within target.  TC-05 – BLE Parent Present:  Goal: Raise the threshold when a parent is nearby.  Setup: Parent device in range (RSSI ≥ −70 dBm). Steps: Simulate normal conversations.  Expected Outcome: T' = T + δ prevents false alarms.  Pass Criteria: Nuisance alerts go down, without missing real risks.  TC-06 – BLE Parent Absent:  Goal: Be more sensitive when the child is alone.  Setup: No parent detected for 3+ minutes.  Steps: Play borderline distress.  Expected Outcome: T' = T − δ increases sensitivity.  Pass Criteria: Higher recall than when parent is present.  TC-07 – Dwell Time Enforcement:

23 |   P a g e  Goal: Prevent alerts from quick noise spikes.  Setup: T = 0.85, dwell = 1–2s, EMA smoothing α ≈ 0.3. Steps: Play short shouts vs sustained distress.  Expected Outcome: Short shouts don’t alert; prolonged distress does. Pass Criteria: 0 false alerts from spike-only cases.  TC-08 – Guard-rail Bypass:  Goal: Always alert when extreme distress is detected.  Setup: Guard-rail active (P(distress) ≥ 0.95), inside safe zone, parent present. Steps: Feed high-confidence distress audio.  Expected Outcome: Alert fires regardless of nudges.  Pass Criteria: 100% of such cases trigger alerts.  TC-09 – Trusted Voice Recognition:  Goal: Don’t alert when a trusted voice is speaking. Setup: Caregiver enrolled.  Steps: Play their speech.  Expected Outcome: High P(trusted), low risk.  Pass Criteria: ≤1% false alerts.  TC-10 – Unknown Voice Risk:  Goal: Increase risk when an unknown adult speaks.  Setup: No matching caregiver enrolled.  Steps: Play an unknown voice with neutral content.  Expected Outcome: δ_unknown applied; risk rises slightly. Pass Criteria: No alert unless distress is also present.

4 |   P a g e  ABSTRACT  Abstract Title:   Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based   Stranger Threat   Detection   for   Child Wearables using Context and On-Device Learning  Children are increasingly outfitted with wearable systems that provide location tracking and panic buttons; however solutions are reactionary and reliant heavily upon cloud-based audio processing that can compromise privacy. This pitch outlines a privacy-preserving audio-based stranger threat detection feature for the child wearable. Two light-weight models run fully off the watch. A Global Danger Sound Model detects acoustic distress events (e.g., screams, crying, threatening speech) by a compressed MobileNet-like convolutional network. A Personal “Circle of Trust” Model authenticates speakers for a determination of whether speech emanates from pre-registered trusted caregivers through on-device voice embeddings (Resemblyzer). Outputs from each model are fed into context (geofence status and distance from a connected parent device through Bluetooth Low Energy) and compute a risk score that triggers an alarm only when the score exceeds a threshold for a dwell time. All audio is stored locally; only a tiny number of metadata (event label, time and rough location) is uploaded to Guardians. An on-device adaptation component clusters repeating unknown speakers and adjusts thresholds to the usual play environment of the youngster. The work will: (i) collect and prepare a balanced dataset of the ensuing classes: a/distress, b/angry speech and c/benign; (ii) design and compress danger and trust models that meet latency (<<50 ms/frame) and power (<<10 % per-day battery) budget; (iii) define performance in laboratory and field trials aiming at >90 % recall and <5 % false alarm rate; and (iv) provide a prototype app for Wear OS. The feasibility of proactive, contextual threat detection at resource-limited wearables without sacrificing user privacy will be demonstrated in the results.  Key Terms:   audio-based threat detection, speaker verification, wearable neural networks, privacy safeguarding, wearable-aware contexts

8 |   P a g e  INTRODUCTION  1.1.   Background & Literature Survey  Stranger danger protection for children is a growing need as children are granted increasing mobility by their parents. Most commercial wearable for children has GPS location, geofencing, and simple SOS buttons but require the child to summon aid personally. Some research prototypes have explored automatic detection of distress from audio cues; many of those systems, though, transmit streamed audio to cloud servers for heavy computation that raises concerns about latency, cost, and privacy [1]. To offset, mobile and wearable design has shifted toward computation on device. An efficient encoder on the wearable device compacts raw input into latent codes at a much lower off-device transmission of data, a notable gain in latency, and preserving privacy [1]. Acoustic event detection has also been researched. YAMNet is a compact model for audio classification that is built off of the model of MobileNet V1, and it incorporates depth wise separable convolutions, allowing it to be very efficient for deployment in handhelds [2]. In speaker verification, there is a simple yet very effective way of obtaining high level voice embeddings through the Resemblyzer library; it makes it very easy for programmers to modify speech regions into vectors in a matter of a few statements [3]. They are typically 256 dimensions [3] and can be compared by cosine similarity. A few open datasets support exploration into the detection of distress and identification of emotion. Audio Signal for Danger Detection of Children and Women has a total of three classes (child danger, woman danger, and normal environment) and has 19,375 one-second audio segments [4], and is a seed set for positive examples for distress. Environmental sounds datasets such as UrbanSound8K (8,732 segments in 10 urban classes of sounds like children playing, siren, and car horn) [5], and ESC-50 (2,000 segments evenly dividing into 50 classes that encompass animal, natural, and household sounds) [6], provide negatives from the environment. To obtain raised-voice surrogates for threatening or anger speech, we borrow from the CREMA- D dataset that has a total of 7,442 segments from 91 performers that represent a variety of emotional states [7], and also from the RAVDESS corpus, a well-experimented multimodal corpus that has a total of 7,356 recordings for which 24 professional actors read sentences in a

Datasets such as SAVEE and TESS also provide some useful training data. These datasets, complemented by some watch microphone datasets collected with permission for a balanced repertoire of distress, anger speech, and common sounds needed for learning models that are not sensitive to this kind of variability. Recent works of environmental sound classification and emotion recognition provide background for our approach. A systematic report about urban sound classification declares that CNNs and DenseNet-based deep learning architectures achieve very high accuracies (97.98%– 99.22%) in UrbanSound8K and ESC-50 datasets, while their models have yet not been validated in real-world deployments [12]. A work that applies the RAVDESS dataset applies log-Mel spectrograms and MFCCs and CNN and LSTM architectures; the networks receive the aggregated (positive, negative, and neutral) sentiments and the network consists of eight convolutional layers [13]. These works indicate the potential of deep learning for our chosen datasets and yet don't appraise privacy-preserving, on-device inference or context-aware fusing, thus highlighting the novelty of the component we propose.

10 |   P a g e  1.2.   Research Gap  Existing child safety wearables focus on location tracking and manual SOS activation. They lack proactive detection of acoustic distress and do not personalize alerts to the child’s trusted caregivers. Many cloud-based audio monitoring solutions upload raw audio, posing privacy risks and introducing latency and connectivity dependencies [1]. Furthermore, children’s play naturally involves shouting and laughter; therefore, a naive screaming detector would generate frequent false alarms. No commercial product currently combines distress detection, speaker verification, contextual information, and on-device learning into a single wearable component. The research gap lies in designing a tiny dual-model pipeline that runs entirely on the watch, adapts to the child’s normal environment, utilizes context cues to reduce false positives, and preserves privacy by keeping raw audio on the device. 14 |   P a g e  3.2   Feature Extraction and Pre-Processing  All windows of the audio will be converted into a log-Mel spectrogram in 32–64 Mel bands. The signal is windowed (e.g., windows of 25 ms at a hop of 10 ms), the Short-Time Fourier Transform is computed and mapped into the Mel scale; the magnitude is also transformed into decibels by a logarithmic calculation. The output time–frequency “image” preserves pitch and temporal structure and is available for CNN input. Ablation experiments may computationally calculate Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs). To introduce a higher level of robustness, we will use common augmentations: additive noise from MUSAN (speech/music/noise), randomness in gain, time stretching, pitch shifting, and time–frequency masks (Spec Augment). They will be parameterized not to alter label semantics and introduce realistic distortions. All pre-processing will be coded in Python using librosa and plugged into TensorFlow data pipelines for efficient learning.  3.3   Global Danger Sound Model  The Global Danger Sound Model estimates the probability that a given 1-s window has distress. It will be trained using MobileNet-V2 or Small MobileNet-V3 backbones, employing inverted residual blocks and depth-wise separable convolutions due to their efficiency. These have proven effective for on-device audio classification (e.g., YAMNet employs a MobileNet V1 [2]). A width multiplier from 0.35 to 0.75 will control parameter count ( ＜ 1 M). The input size (e.g., 64×96) is 64 Mel bands by 96 time frames. Loss and Training: Because events of worry are rarer than negatives, a focal loss (γ = 2) or class-weighted cross-entropy loss will minimize class imbalance. Training will be done twice: pre-training over the big publicly available datasets, and fine-tuning over the consent watch dataset through k-fold cross-validation. Early stopping based on the validation false alarm rate will prevent overfitting. Augmented data will foster diversity. Model Compression: To meet the watch’s energy and memory constraints, we will apply pruning and quantization-aware training (QAT). Pruning zeros out near-zero weights and retains sparse matrices that can be sparsely represented; QAT compacts weights and activations into 8-bit integers at the expense of very minimal loss in accuracy. The compressed TFLite model (~500 kB) will be validated through the official benchmark.

15 |   P a g e  3.4   Personal “Circle of Trust” Model  Speaker verification confirms that the system differentiates between well-known caregivers and unknown voices. At enrollment, each caregiver speaks 3–5 statements (5–10 s). Audio passes through a speaker encoder and produces embedding; Resemblyzer provides 256- dimensional embeddings and makes it easy for developers to represent segments of audio as vectors [3]. Alternatively, use the Speech Brain ECAPATDNN model (192-D). A centroid (mean vector) is computed for each speaker. At inference, after detection of voice activity, the system computes the last speech segment's embedding and computes cosine similarity for each enrolled centroid; maximum similarity is converted into P(trusted) by a calibrated sigmoid. If no speech is detected (silence), P(trusted) = 1 so that no penalty is assigned for silence. Storage and Security: We maintain only embeddings and centroids locally on the device and store them securely through the Android Keystore or Keychain for iOS. We save no raw audio. Enrollment operations require parent authentication. Voice Activity Detection (VAD): A light-weight VAD module (e.g., WebRTC GMM-based or Silero NN-based) gates the speaker verification chain so that it does not compute embeddings when there is no speech at all. This ensures that the trust model is only triggered when there is speech.

The instantaneous risk values are processed through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with smoothing factor   α   ≈ 0 . 3 to avoid flickering alerts. A dynamic threshold   T   is set (e.g., 0.85) and modified by context:  •   Geofence: If the child is inside trusted areas (home or school), the threshold increases slightly (∆   >   0). Outside safe zones, the threshold decreases (−∆) to favor detection.  •   Parent BLE proximity: The presence of a paired parent device via BLE nudges the threshold upwards ( δ >   0). Absence nudges it downwards (− δ ).  An alert is triggered only when the smoothed risk exceeds the threshold for a dwell time (e.g., 1–2 s). The alert payload includes the event label, risk confidence, and coarse location; no audio is transmitted.  Figure 1.1: Risk Fusion and Thresholding

17 |   P a g e  3.6   On-Device Learning and Adaptation  The system continuously adjusts by learning from its world without transferring audio. Trusted Voice Expansion:   Repeatedly observed embeddings of unknown speakers that appear around the child are grouped by Minibatch K-Means or DBSCAN. If the cluster is observed over more than one session, the parent is asked for permission to move the voice into the trusted list. Once approved, a few embeddings are collected and the centroid is saved securely.  Baseline Adaptation:   To reduce false alarms during normal play, streaming statistics (e.g., energy and spectral centroid) are tracked using exponential smoothing or streaming quantile estimators. If the current audio is like the baseline profile, the risk score decreases slightly. These adjustments are conservative, not to suppress the real threat. 4 |   P a g e  ABSTRACT  Abstract Title:   Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based   Stranger Threat   Detection   for   Child Wearables using Context and On-Device Learning  Children are increasingly outfitted with wearable systems that provide location tracking and panic buttons; however solutions are reactionary and reliant heavily upon cloud-based audio processing that can compromise privacy. This pitch outlines a privacy-preserving audio-based stranger threat detection feature for the child wearable. Two light-weight models run fully off the watch. A Global Danger Sound Model detects acoustic distress events (e.g., screams, crying, threatening speech) by a compressed MobileNet-like convolutional network. A Personal “Circle of Trust” Model authenticates speakers for a determination of whether speech emanates from pre-registered trusted caregivers through on-device voice embeddings (Resemblyzer). Outputs from each model are fed into context (geofence status and distance from a connected parent device through Bluetooth Low Energy) and compute a risk score that triggers an alarm only when the score exceeds a threshold for a dwell time. All audio is stored locally; only a tiny number of metadata (event label, time and rough location) is uploaded to Guardians. An on-device adaptation component clusters repeating unknown speakers and adjusts thresholds to the usual play environment of the youngster. The work will: (i) collect and prepare a balanced dataset of the ensuing classes: a/distress, b/angry speech and c/benign; (ii) design and compress danger and trust models that meet latency (<<50 ms/frame) and power (<<10 % per-day battery) budget; (iii) define performance in laboratory and field trials aiming at >90 % recall and <5 % false alarm rate; and (iv) provide a prototype app for Wear OS. The feasibility of proactive, contextual threat detection at resource-limited wearables without sacrificing user privacy will be demonstrated in the results.  Key Terms:   audio-based threat detection, speaker verification, wearable neural networks, privacy safeguarding, wearable-aware contexts

8 |   P a g e  INTRODUCTION  1.1.   Background & Literature Survey  Stranger danger protection for children is a growing need as children are granted increasing mobility by their parents. Most commercial wearable for children has GPS location, geofencing, and simple SOS buttons but require the child to summon aid personally. Some research prototypes have explored automatic detection of distress from audio cues; many of those systems, though, transmit streamed audio to cloud servers for heavy computation that raises concerns about latency, cost, and privacy [1]. To offset, mobile and wearable design has shifted toward computation on device. An efficient encoder on the wearable device compacts raw input into latent codes at a much lower off-device transmission of data, a notable gain in latency, and preserving privacy [1]. Acoustic event detection has also been researched. YAMNet is a compact model for audio classification that is built off of the model of MobileNet V1, and it incorporates depth wise separable convolutions, allowing it to be very efficient for deployment in handhelds [2]. In speaker verification, there is a simple yet very effective way of obtaining high level voice embeddings through the Resemblyzer library; it makes it very easy for programmers to modify speech regions into vectors in a matter of a few statements [3]. They are typically 256 dimensions [3] and can be compared by cosine similarity. A few open datasets support exploration into the detection of distress and identification of emotion. Audio Signal for Danger Detection of Children and Women has a total of three classes (child danger, woman danger, and normal environment) and has 19,375 one-second audio segments [4], and is a seed set for positive examples for distress. Environmental sounds datasets such as UrbanSound8K (8,732 segments in 10 urban classes of sounds like children playing, siren, and car horn) [5], and ESC-50 (2,000 segments evenly dividing into 50 classes that encompass animal, natural, and household sounds) [6], provide negatives from the environment. To obtain raised-voice surrogates for threatening or anger speech, we borrow from the CREMA- D dataset that has a total of 7,442 segments from 91 performers that represent a variety of emotional states [7], and also from the RAVDESS corpus, a well-experimented multimodal corpus that has a total of 7,356 recordings for which 24 professional actors read sentences in a

9 |   P a g e  total of eight emotional states [8]. To attain complete multi-label diversity for sounds, FSD50K provides more than 51,000 audio segments that are labeled for a total of 200 classes [9]. Datasets such as SAVEE and TESS also provide some useful training data. Surrey Audio-Visual Expressed Emotion (SAVEE) contains 480 phonetically balanced British English speech utterances by four male speakers reproducing seven emotional states; we comment that based on the TensorFlow dataset description, only audio is utilized and the learning, validation, and testing splits are samples from speakers other than those in the learning and validation splits [10]. The Toronto Emotional Speech Set (TESS) contains 200 target words spoken by two actresses (26 and 64 years old) in seven emotional states (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, pleasant surprise, sadness, and neutral), yielding a total of 2,800 stimuli [11]. These datasets, complemented by some watch microphone datasets collected with permission for a balanced repertoire of distress, anger speech, and common sounds needed for learning models that are not sensitive to this kind of variability. Recent works of environmental sound classification and emotion recognition provide background for our approach. A systematic report about urban sound classification declares that CNNs and DenseNet-based deep learning architectures achieve very high accuracies (97.98%– 99.22%) in UrbanSound8K and ESC-50 datasets, while their models have yet not been validated in real-world deployments [12]. A work that applies the RAVDESS dataset applies log-Mel spectrograms and MFCCs and CNN and LSTM architectures; the networks receive the aggregated (positive, negative, and neutral) sentiments and the network consists of eight convolutional layers [13]. These works indicate the potential of deep learning for our chosen datasets and yet don't appraise privacy-preserving, on-device inference or context-aware fusing, thus highlighting the novelty of the component we propose.

10 |   P a g e  1.2.   Research Gap  Existing child safety wearables focus on location tracking and manual SOS activation. They lack proactive detection of acoustic distress and do not personalize alerts to the child’s trusted caregivers. Many cloud-based audio monitoring solutions upload raw audio, posing privacy risks and introducing latency and connectivity dependencies [1]. Furthermore, children’s play naturally involves shouting and laughter; therefore, a naive screaming detector would generate frequent false alarms. No commercial product currently combines distress detection, speaker verification, contextual information, and on-device learning into a single wearable component. The research gap lies in designing a tiny dual-model pipeline that runs entirely on the watch, adapts to the child’s normal environment, utilizes context cues to reduce false positives, and preserves privacy by keeping raw audio on the device. 11 |   P a g e  1.3.   Research Problem  Design a stranger-threat detection component for children's wearables that (a) makes real-time predictions of likelihood of acoustic distress, (b) verifies that speech is from registered trusted voices through the device, (c) combine these likelihoods with contextual clues (geofence and parent device distance) to compute a risk score, (d) adapt thresholds and trusted voices through on-device learning, and (e) operates under hard latency (<50 ms per frame), power (<10 % day- per-day battery), and false alarm (<5 %) limits. The system should operate without uploading raw audio off the watch and should provide minimal metadata to guardians to preserve privacy  2.   OBJECTIVES  2.1 Main Objective  To build, deploy, and evaluate a privacy-friendly voice-based stranger threat detection for kid wear that actively detects distress incidents, verifies trusted voices, and applies context to deliver credible alerts while maintaining on-device privacy  2.2   Specific Objectives  •   Collecting and Curating the Dataset: Assemble a balanced dataset from publicly available emotional/distress databases (Women & Children Danger, Audio Set “Screaming”, RAVDESS, CREMA-D, SAVEE, TESS), environmental sounds datasets (UrbanSound8K, ESC-50, FSD50K), and a restricted, consenting watch-microphone dataset. Prepare all audio into mono 16 kHz, 1-s windows with 50 % overlap and compute log-Mel spectrograms.  •   Global Danger Sound Model: Design a light-weight model from MobileNetV2/V3 that has <1 M parameters. Fine-tune using class-balanced loss functions, data augmentations, and watch- quality data-based fine-tuning. Prune the model and apply quantization-aware training to generate an 8-bit TFLite model that has less than a 50 ms per-frame inference time.  •   Personal Circle of Trust Model: Integrate a speaker verification system using Resemblyzer or Speech Brain ECAPA-TDNN embeddings. Develop a voice enrollment procedure for caregivers and translate cosine similarity into P(trusted voice) using calibrated sigmoid functions. Keep embeddings safely stored on the device using Android Keystore or iOS Keychain.  •   Risk Smoothing and Fusion: Define the risk calculation Risk = wd · P(distress) · (1 − P(trusted)) + δunknown and smooth by an exponential moving average. Include context nudges based on geofencing and BLE proximity to adjust the alert threshold.

12 |   P a g e  •   On-Device Adaptation: Develop clustering methods (Mini Batch K-Means or DBSCAN) that detect long-lived unknown voices and alert parents to add new trusted speakers. Maintain online statistics of environmental energy noises to adapt thresholds to typical play.  •   Implementation and Integration: Build an end-to-end pipeline in WearOS. Gate the pipeline with Voice Activity Detection (WebRTC/Silero), run models with TFLite and the XNNPACK delegate, and interleave Android Location and BLE APIs for context. Measure computation and power usage with Android Studio Power Profiler.  •   Evaluation: Establish quantitative specifications (recall >90 %, FAR <5 %, latency ≤2 s, battery impact <10 %) and conduct experiments through controlled datasets and field trials. Get guardian feedback for usability and nuisance alarm.  •   Deliverables: Make a working wearable device prototype, a smartphone sidekick app, an evaluation report, and deliverable-ready documentation for potential future deployment or commercialization.

13 |   P a g e  3.   METHODOLOGY  3.1   Datasets and Data Collection  To train robust models, the project will combine multiple open datasets (Table 1.1) along with a bespoke watch-microphone dataset recorded under consent.  Dataset Name   Classes / Content   Clips / Duration   Purpose   Citation  Women & Children in Danger  Child danger, woman danger, normal  19,375   Distress examples   [4]  Audio Set “Screaming”  Screaming, other   1000   Distress examples   [9]  UrbanSound8K   10 (e.g., kids playing, siren)  8732   Normal backgrounds  [5]  ESC-50   50 (e.g., animal, home sounds)  2000   Normal backgrounds  [6]  FSD50K   200 sound types   7356   Angry/scary talk   [8]  SAVEE   7 emotions   480   Emotion training   [10]  TESS   7 emotions   2800   Emotion training   [11]  Watch Mic Data   Distress, normal play  500   Device tuning   N/A  Table 1.2 : Dataset Summary  All datasets shall be resampled into mono at a rate of 16 kHz, windowed into segments of 1 s width with 50 % overlap, and normalized. Positive examples of distress shall be screams, crying, speech during anger, and fearful faces; negative examples shall be ordinary environmental sounds and natural speech. The consent watch dataset shall be collected after getting ethical clearance and shall comprise sentences spoken by caregivers and children playing for fine-tuning the models for the target device's acoustics.

14 |   P a g e  3.2   Feature Extraction and Pre-Processing  All windows of the audio will be converted into a log-Mel spectrogram in 32–64 Mel bands. The signal is windowed (e.g., windows of 25 ms at a hop of 10 ms), the Short-Time Fourier Transform is computed and mapped into the Mel scale; the magnitude is also transformed into decibels by a logarithmic calculation. The output time–frequency “image” preserves pitch and temporal structure and is available for CNN input. Ablation experiments may computationally calculate Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs). To introduce a higher level of robustness, we will use common augmentations: additive noise from MUSAN (speech/music/noise), randomness in gain, time stretching, pitch shifting, and time–frequency masks (Spec Augment). They will be parameterized not to alter label semantics and introduce realistic distortions. All pre-processing will be coded in Python using librosa and plugged into TensorFlow data pipelines for efficient learning.  3.3   Global Danger Sound Model  The Global Danger Sound Model estimates the probability that a given 1-s window has distress. It will be trained using MobileNet-V2 or Small MobileNet-V3 backbones, employing inverted residual blocks and depth-wise separable convolutions due to their efficiency. These have proven effective for on-device audio classification (e.g., YAMNet employs a MobileNet V1 [2]). A width multiplier from 0.35 to 0.75 will control parameter count ( ＜ 1 M). The input size (e.g., 64×96) is 64 Mel bands by 96 time frames. Loss and Training: Because events of worry are rarer than negatives, a focal loss (γ = 2) or class-weighted cross-entropy loss will minimize class imbalance. Training will be done twice: pre-training over the big publicly available datasets, and fine-tuning over the consent watch dataset through k-fold cross-validation. Early stopping based on the validation false alarm rate will prevent overfitting. Augmented data will foster diversity. Model Compression: To meet the watch’s energy and memory constraints, we will apply pruning and quantization-aware training (QAT). Pruning zeros out near-zero weights and retains sparse matrices that can be sparsely represented; QAT compacts weights and activations into 8-bit integers at the expense of very minimal loss in accuracy. The compressed TFLite model (~500 kB) will be validated through the official benchmark.

15 |   P a g e  3.4   Personal “Circle of Trust” Model  Speaker verification confirms that the system differentiates between well-known caregivers and unknown voices. At enrollment, each caregiver speaks 3–5 statements (5–10 s). Audio passes through a speaker encoder and produces embedding; Resemblyzer provides 256- dimensional embeddings and makes it easy for developers to represent segments of audio as vectors [3]. Alternatively, use the Speech Brain ECAPATDNN model (192-D). A centroid (mean vector) is computed for each speaker. At inference, after detection of voice activity, the system computes the last speech segment's embedding and computes cosine similarity for each enrolled centroid; maximum similarity is converted into P(trusted) by a calibrated sigmoid. If no speech is detected (silence), P(trusted) = 1 so that no penalty is assigned for silence. Storage and Security: We maintain only embeddings and centroids locally on the device and store them securely through the Android Keystore or Keychain for iOS. We save no raw audio. Enrollment operations require parent authentication. Voice Activity Detection (VAD): A light-weight VAD module (e.g., WebRTC GMM-based or Silero NN-based) gates the speaker verification chain so that it does not compute embeddings when there is no speech at all. This ensures that the trust model is only triggered when there is speech.

16 |   P a g e  3.5   Risk Fusion and Smoothing  For each audio window, the watch computes:  Risk   =   w d   ·   P (distress) · (1 −   P (trusted))+   δ unknown ,  where   w d   is a weight (initially 1.0) and   δ unknown   is a small penalty (e.g., 0.05–0.15) applied when speech is detected but not recognized as trusted. The instantaneous risk values are processed through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with smoothing factor   α   ≈ 0 . 3 to avoid flickering alerts. A dynamic threshold   T   is set (e.g., 0.85) and modified by context:  •   Geofence: If the child is inside trusted areas (home or school), the threshold increases slightly (∆   >   0). Outside safe zones, the threshold decreases (−∆) to favor detection.  •   Parent BLE proximity: The presence of a paired parent device via BLE nudges the threshold upwards ( δ >   0). Absence nudges it downwards (− δ ).  An alert is triggered only when the smoothed risk exceeds the threshold for a dwell time (e.g., 1–2 s). The alert payload includes the event label, risk confidence, and coarse location; no audio is transmitted.  Figure 1.1: Risk Fusion and Thresholding

17 |   P a g e  3.6   On-Device Learning and Adaptation  The system continuously adjusts by learning from its world without transferring audio. Trusted Voice Expansion:   Repeatedly observed embeddings of unknown speakers that appear around the child are grouped by Minibatch K-Means or DBSCAN. If the cluster is observed over more than one session, the parent is asked for permission to move the voice into the trusted list. Once approved, a few embeddings are collected and the centroid is saved securely.  Baseline Adaptation:   To reduce false alarms during normal play, streaming statistics (e.g., energy and spectral centroid) are tracked using exponential smoothing or streaming quantile estimators. If the current audio is like the baseline profile, the risk score decreases slightly. These adjustments are conservative, not to suppress the real threat.  Figure 1.2: Post-Deployment Learning Workflow

18 |   P a g e  3.7 System Implementation Plan  Figure 1.3: High-Level System Architecture  •   Audio Capture:   Continuous recording from the watch mic into a ring buffer. We process in 1-second frames at a 0.5-second hop.  •   Voice Activity Detection:   A tiny VAD module checks for speech or a loud event in frame. If not, it sleeps.  •   Feature Extraction:   Log-Mel spectrogram computation runs locally on device using optimized C++/TFLite.  •   Global Danger Model:   The compacted MobileNet model forecasts   P(distress) .  •   Speaker Verification:   If there is speech, the trust model computes embeddings and compares them to trusted centroids to generate   P(trusted) .  •   Risk Fusion:   Combines probabilities, applies an unknown voice penalty and context- based nudges (like geofence & BLE), then smooths the result over time.  •   Alert Manager:   When risk stays above the threshold for a set duration, it sends an alert via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi to the guardian’s phone. The app displays the alert and optional map location.

19 |   P a g e  •   On-Device Learning:   Maintains embedding buffers and baseline statistics, triggers prompts for adding new trusted voices, and adapts thresholds as needed.  Implementation Tools:  •   Software:  TensorFlow/Keras for model development TensorFlow Lite with XNNPACK delegate for on-device inference WebRTC VAD or Silero VAD Android APIs for audio, geofencing, and BLE scanning PyTorch or Speech Brain for alternative speaker encoders scikit-learn for clustering  •   Hardware:  Wear OS smartwatches (e.g., Snapdragon Wear 4100 or newer) Android smartphone for the   parent device  GPU-enabled development workstation for training and experimentation  3.8   Handling Offline Scenarios and Connectivity Issues.  The solution is tolerant of infrequent internet connections. While offline, all important threat alerts are stored locally on the smartwatch. The alert is time-stamped and queued to be sent to the backend server as soon as the device gets back online to ensure that no alert is lost. To enable a timely response in offline scenarios, the device has a local, attention- seeking audio alarm that can alert individuals in close proximity.

20 |   P a g e  4.   PROJECT REQUIREMENTS  4.1 Functional Requirements (FR)  FR-1: Recording in-device and Voice-Activated Device  Capture permanently mono 16 kHz audio from the watch. Use a light-weight VAD (“speech / loud event”) gate to decide when downstream models should run in order to maintain power.  FR-2: Global Threat Tone Model  Run a tiny CNN (e.g., MobileNet-V2/V3-Small TFLite int8) on log-Mel features to estimate P(distress) ∈ [0,1] for 1 s windows (50% overlap).  FR-3: One "Circle of Trust" (speaker verification)  When speech is detected by VAD, compute an on-device embedding and estimate P(trusted voice) ∈ [0,1] by cosine-similarity to enrolled caregivers (no raw audio is retained).  FR-4: Risk fusion & smoothing  Compute per-window Risk = wd   ⋅   P(distress) ⋅ (1−P(trusted))+δ unknown. Apply EMA smoothing (α≈0.3, 2–3 s). Trigger alerts only if EMA(Risk) > dynamic threshold T′ for dwell 1– 2 s.  FR-5: Location/geofencing context  Maintain trusted geofences (e.g., Home, School; radius ≥100 m; use DWELL). Inside safe zones: T′=T+Δ (Δ≈+0.05…+0.08). Outside: T′=T−Δ (Δ≈0.03…0.06). Store only coarse place labels in alerts.  FR-6: BLE parent-device proximity  Conduct brief scan spurts using Bluetooth LE Scanner filters (parent MAC/UUID). If parent is present (RSSI ≥ −70 dBm observed ≤60 s): T′=T + δ (δ≈+0.02…+0.05). If not present ≥3  FR-7: Alerts & guardian app  Send alerts only in metadata (label, confidence, timestamp, coarse location, parent-near flag). Supply acknowledge/snooze on the guardian device. No audio leaves the watch.

21 |   P a g e  FR-8: Privacy & security  Store only embeddings, centroids, and light-weight statistics. Encrypt at rest (Keystore/Keychain). Authenticate enrollment/management operations.  FR-9: Enrollment & configuration  Allow caregiver registration (3–5 concise statements), geofencing setup, parent-device synchronization, and parameters for safe tuning (T, Δ, δ, dwell).  FR-10: On-device learning  (a) Expansion of trusted-voice: cluster repeat unknown embeddings; with parental permission, introduce as trusted. (b) Modality adaptation of baseline: store EMA of energy/bands to slightly de-weight risk during normal play (never to zero). NFR-4 (Precision):  In field testing, the system should identify at least 90% of distress cases (recall), while keeping false alarms (false alarm rate) below 5%.  NFR-5 (Robustness):  The system should handle everyday background noise (like sirens, playgrounds, traffic) and multiple languages effectively. NFR-6 (Security):  Use hardware-backed encryption keys when available, and enforce role-based access control for tasks like enrolling caregivers or managing settings. 4 |   P a g e  ABSTRACT  Abstract Title:   Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based   Stranger Threat   Detection   for   Child Wearables using Context and On-Device Learning  Children are increasingly outfitted with wearable systems that provide location tracking and panic buttons; however solutions are reactionary and reliant heavily upon cloud-based audio processing that can compromise privacy. This pitch outlines a privacy-preserving audio-based stranger threat detection feature for the child wearable. Two light-weight models run fully off the watch. A Global Danger Sound Model detects acoustic distress events (e.g., screams, crying, threatening speech) by a compressed MobileNet-like convolutional network. A Personal “Circle of Trust” Model authenticates speakers for a determination of whether speech emanates from pre-registered trusted caregivers through on-device voice embeddings (Resemblyzer). Outputs from each model are fed into context (geofence status and distance from a connected parent device through Bluetooth Low Energy) and compute a risk score that triggers an alarm only when the score exceeds a threshold for a dwell time. All audio is stored locally; only a tiny number of metadata (event label, time and rough location) is uploaded to Guardians. An on-device adaptation component clusters repeating unknown speakers and adjusts thresholds to the usual play environment of the youngster. The work will: (i) collect and prepare a balanced dataset of the ensuing classes: a/distress, b/angry speech and c/benign; (ii) design and compress danger and trust models that meet latency (<<50 ms/frame) and power (<<10 % per-day battery) budget; (iii) define performance in laboratory and field trials aiming at >90 % recall and <5 % false alarm rate; and (iv) provide a prototype app for Wear OS. The feasibility of proactive, contextual threat detection at resource-limited wearables without sacrificing user privacy will be demonstrated in the results.  Key Terms:   audio-based threat detection, speaker verification, wearable neural networks, privacy safeguarding, wearable-aware contexts

8 |   P a g e  INTRODUCTION  1.1.   Background & Literature Survey  Stranger danger protection for children is a growing need as children are granted increasing mobility by their parents. Most commercial wearable for children has GPS location, geofencing, and simple SOS buttons but require the child to summon aid personally. Some research prototypes have explored automatic detection of distress from audio cues; many of those systems, though, transmit streamed audio to cloud servers for heavy computation that raises concerns about latency, cost, and privacy [1]. To offset, mobile and wearable design has shifted toward computation on device. An efficient encoder on the wearable device compacts raw input into latent codes at a much lower off-device transmission of data, a notable gain in latency, and preserving privacy [1]. Acoustic event detection has also been researched. YAMNet is a compact model for audio classification that is built off of the model of MobileNet V1, and it incorporates depth wise separable convolutions, allowing it to be very efficient for deployment in handhelds [2]. In speaker verification, there is a simple yet very effective way of obtaining high level voice embeddings through the Resemblyzer library; it makes it very easy for programmers to modify speech regions into vectors in a matter of a few statements [3]. They are typically 256 dimensions [3] and can be compared by cosine similarity. A few open datasets support exploration into the detection of distress and identification of emotion. Audio Signal for Danger Detection of Children and Women has a total of three classes (child danger, woman danger, and normal environment) and has 19,375 one-second audio segments [4], and is a seed set for positive examples for distress. Environmental sounds datasets such as UrbanSound8K (8,732 segments in 10 urban classes of sounds like children playing, siren, and car horn) [5], and ESC-50 (2,000 segments evenly dividing into 50 classes that encompass animal, natural, and household sounds) [6], provide negatives from the environment. To obtain raised-voice surrogates for threatening or anger speech, we borrow from the CREMA- D dataset that has a total of 7,442 segments from 91 performers that represent a variety of emotional states [7], and also from the RAVDESS corpus, a well-experimented multimodal corpus that has a total of 7,356 recordings for which 24 professional actors read sentences in a

9 |   P a g e  total of eight emotional states [8]. To attain complete multi-label diversity for sounds, FSD50K provides more than 51,000 audio segments that are labeled for a total of 200 classes [9]. Datasets such as SAVEE and TESS also provide some useful training data. Surrey Audio-Visual Expressed Emotion (SAVEE) contains 480 phonetically balanced British English speech utterances by four male speakers reproducing seven emotional states; we comment that based on the TensorFlow dataset description, only audio is utilized and the learning, validation, and testing splits are samples from speakers other than those in the learning and validation splits [10]. The Toronto Emotional Speech Set (TESS) contains 200 target words spoken by two actresses (26 and 64 years old) in seven emotional states (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, pleasant surprise, sadness, and neutral), yielding a total of 2,800 stimuli [11]. These datasets, complemented by some watch microphone datasets collected with permission for a balanced repertoire of distress, anger speech, and common sounds needed for learning models that are not sensitive to this kind of variability. Recent works of environmental sound classification and emotion recognition provide background for our approach. A systematic report about urban sound classification declares that CNNs and DenseNet-based deep learning architectures achieve very high accuracies (97.98%– 99.22%) in UrbanSound8K and ESC-50 datasets, while their models have yet not been validated in real-world deployments [12]. A work that applies the RAVDESS dataset applies log-Mel spectrograms and MFCCs and CNN and LSTM architectures; the networks receive the aggregated (positive, negative, and neutral) sentiments and the network consists of eight convolutional layers [13]. These works indicate the potential of deep learning for our chosen datasets and yet don't appraise privacy-preserving, on-device inference or context-aware fusing, thus highlighting the novelty of the component we propose.

10 |   P a g e  1.2.   Research Gap  Existing child safety wearables focus on location tracking and manual SOS activation. They lack proactive detection of acoustic distress and do not personalize alerts to the child’s trusted caregivers. Many cloud-based audio monitoring solutions upload raw audio, posing privacy risks and introducing latency and connectivity dependencies [1]. Furthermore, children’s play naturally involves shouting and laughter; therefore, a naive screaming detector would generate frequent false alarms. No commercial product currently combines distress detection, speaker verification, contextual information, and on-device learning into a single wearable component. The research gap lies in designing a tiny dual-model pipeline that runs entirely on the watch, adapts to the child’s normal environment, utilizes context cues to reduce false positives, and preserves privacy by keeping raw audio on the device. 11 |   P a g e  1.3.   Research Problem  Design a stranger-threat detection component for children's wearables that (a) makes real-time predictions of likelihood of acoustic distress, (b) verifies that speech is from registered trusted voices through the device, (c) combine these likelihoods with contextual clues (geofence and parent device distance) to compute a risk score, (d) adapt thresholds and trusted voices through on-device learning, and (e) operates under hard latency (<50 ms per frame), power (<10 % day- per-day battery), and false alarm (<5 %) limits. The system should operate without uploading raw audio off the watch and should provide minimal metadata to guardians to preserve privacy  2.   OBJECTIVES  2.1 Main Objective  To build, deploy, and evaluate a privacy-friendly voice-based stranger threat detection for kid wear that actively detects distress incidents, verifies trusted voices, and applies context to deliver credible alerts while maintaining on-device privacy  2.2   Specific Objectives  •   Collecting and Curating the Dataset: Assemble a balanced dataset from publicly available emotional/distress databases (Women & Children Danger, Audio Set “Screaming”, RAVDESS, CREMA-D, SAVEE, TESS), environmental sounds datasets (UrbanSound8K, ESC-50, FSD50K), and a restricted, consenting watch-microphone dataset. Prepare all audio into mono 16 kHz, 1-s windows with 50 % overlap and compute log-Mel spectrograms.  •   Global Danger Sound Model: Design a light-weight model from MobileNetV2/V3 that has <1 M parameters. Fine-tune using class-balanced loss functions, data augmentations, and watch- quality data-based fine-tuning. Prune the model and apply quantization-aware training to generate an 8-bit TFLite model that has less than a 50 ms per-frame inference time.  •   Personal Circle of Trust Model: Integrate a speaker verification system using Resemblyzer or Speech Brain ECAPA-TDNN embeddings. Develop a voice enrollment procedure for caregivers and translate cosine similarity into P(trusted voice) using calibrated sigmoid functions. Keep embeddings safely stored on the device using Android Keystore or iOS Keychain.  •   Risk Smoothing and Fusion: Define the risk calculation Risk = wd · P(distress) · (1 − P(trusted)) + δunknown and smooth by an exponential moving average. Include context nudges based on geofencing and BLE proximity to adjust the alert threshold.

12 |   P a g e  •   On-Device Adaptation: Develop clustering methods (Mini Batch K-Means or DBSCAN) that detect long-lived unknown voices and alert parents to add new trusted speakers. Maintain online statistics of environmental energy noises to adapt thresholds to typical play.  •   Implementation and Integration: Build an end-to-end pipeline in WearOS. Gate the pipeline with Voice Activity Detection (WebRTC/Silero), run models with TFLite and the XNNPACK delegate, and interleave Android Location and BLE APIs for context. Measure computation and power usage with Android Studio Power Profiler.  •   Evaluation: Establish quantitative specifications (recall >90 %, FAR <5 %, latency ≤2 s, battery impact <10 %) and conduct experiments through controlled datasets and field trials. Get guardian feedback for usability and nuisance alarm.  •   Deliverables: Make a working wearable device prototype, a smartphone sidekick app, an evaluation report, and deliverable-ready documentation for potential future deployment or commercialization.

13 |   P a g e  3.   METHODOLOGY  3.1   Datasets and Data Collection  To train robust models, the project will combine multiple open datasets (Table 1.1) along with a bespoke watch-microphone dataset recorded under consent.  Dataset Name   Classes / Content   Clips / Duration   Purpose   Citation  Women & Children in Danger  Child danger, woman danger, normal  19,375   Distress examples   [4]  Audio Set “Screaming”  Screaming, other   1000   Distress examples   [9]  UrbanSound8K   10 (e.g., kids playing, siren)  8732   Normal backgrounds  [5]  ESC-50   50 (e.g., animal, home sounds)  2000   Normal backgrounds  [6]  FSD50K   200 sound types   7356   Angry/scary talk   [8]  SAVEE   7 emotions   480   Emotion training   [10]  TESS   7 emotions   2800   Emotion training   [11]  Watch Mic Data   Distress, normal play  500   Device tuning   N/A  Table 1.2 : Dataset Summary  All datasets shall be resampled into mono at a rate of 16 kHz, windowed into segments of 1 s width with 50 % overlap, and normalized. Positive examples of distress shall be screams, crying, speech during anger, and fearful faces; negative examples shall be ordinary environmental sounds and natural speech. The consent watch dataset shall be collected after getting ethical clearance and shall comprise sentences spoken by caregivers and children playing for fine-tuning the models for the target device's acoustics.

14 |   P a g e  3.2   Feature Extraction and Pre-Processing  All windows of the audio will be converted into a log-Mel spectrogram in 32–64 Mel bands. The signal is windowed (e.g., windows of 25 ms at a hop of 10 ms), the Short-Time Fourier Transform is computed and mapped into the Mel scale; the magnitude is also transformed into decibels by a logarithmic calculation. The output time–frequency “image” preserves pitch and temporal structure and is available for CNN input. Ablation experiments may computationally calculate Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs). To introduce a higher level of robustness, we will use common augmentations: additive noise from MUSAN (speech/music/noise), randomness in gain, time stretching, pitch shifting, and time–frequency masks (Spec Augment). They will be parameterized not to alter label semantics and introduce realistic distortions. All pre-processing will be coded in Python using librosa and plugged into TensorFlow data pipelines for efficient learning.  3.3   Global Danger Sound Model  The Global Danger Sound Model estimates the probability that a given 1-s window has distress. It will be trained using MobileNet-V2 or Small MobileNet-V3 backbones, employing inverted residual blocks and depth-wise separable convolutions due to their efficiency. These have proven effective for on-device audio classification (e.g., YAMNet employs a MobileNet V1 [2]). A width multiplier from 0.35 to 0.75 will control parameter count ( ＜ 1 M). The input size (e.g., 64×96) is 64 Mel bands by 96 time frames. Loss and Training: Because events of worry are rarer than negatives, a focal loss (γ = 2) or class-weighted cross-entropy loss will minimize class imbalance. Training will be done twice: pre-training over the big publicly available datasets, and fine-tuning over the consent watch dataset through k-fold cross-validation. Early stopping based on the validation false alarm rate will prevent overfitting. Augmented data will foster diversity. Model Compression: To meet the watch’s energy and memory constraints, we will apply pruning and quantization-aware training (QAT). Pruning zeros out near-zero weights and retains sparse matrices that can be sparsely represented; QAT compacts weights and activations into 8-bit integers at the expense of very minimal loss in accuracy. The compressed TFLite model (~500 kB) will be validated through the official benchmark.

15 |   P a g e  3.4   Personal “Circle of Trust” Model  Speaker verification confirms that the system differentiates between well-known caregivers and unknown voices. At enrollment, each caregiver speaks 3–5 statements (5–10 s). Audio passes through a speaker encoder and produces embedding; Resemblyzer provides 256- dimensional embeddings and makes it easy for developers to represent segments of audio as vectors [3]. Alternatively, use the Speech Brain ECAPATDNN model (192-D). A centroid (mean vector) is computed for each speaker. At inference, after detection of voice activity, the system computes the last speech segment's embedding and computes cosine similarity for each enrolled centroid; maximum similarity is converted into P(trusted) by a calibrated sigmoid. If no speech is detected (silence), P(trusted) = 1 so that no penalty is assigned for silence. Storage and Security: We maintain only embeddings and centroids locally on the device and store them securely through the Android Keystore or Keychain for iOS. We save no raw audio. Enrollment operations require parent authentication. Voice Activity Detection (VAD): A light-weight VAD module (e.g., WebRTC GMM-based or Silero NN-based) gates the speaker verification chain so that it does not compute embeddings when there is no speech at all. This ensures that the trust model is only triggered when there is speech.

16 |   P a g e  3.5   Risk Fusion and Smoothing  For each audio window, the watch computes:  Risk   =   w d   ·   P (distress) · (1 −   P (trusted))+   δ unknown ,  where   w d   is a weight (initially 1.0) and   δ unknown   is a small penalty (e.g., 0.05–0.15) applied when speech is detected but not recognized as trusted. The instantaneous risk values are processed through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with smoothing factor   α   ≈ 0 . 3 to avoid flickering alerts. A dynamic threshold   T   is set (e.g., 0.85) and modified by context:  •   Geofence: If the child is inside trusted areas (home or school), the threshold increases slightly (∆   >   0). Outside safe zones, the threshold decreases (−∆) to favor detection.  •   Parent BLE proximity: The presence of a paired parent device via BLE nudges the threshold upwards ( δ >   0). Absence nudges it downwards (− δ ).  An alert is triggered only when the smoothed risk exceeds the threshold for a dwell time (e.g., 1–2 s). The alert payload includes the event label, risk confidence, and coarse location; no audio is transmitted.  Figure 1.1: Risk Fusion and Thresholding

17 |   P a g e  3.6   On-Device Learning and Adaptation  The system continuously adjusts by learning from its world without transferring audio. Trusted Voice Expansion:   Repeatedly observed embeddings of unknown speakers that appear around the child are grouped by Minibatch K-Means or DBSCAN. If the cluster is observed over more than one session, the parent is asked for permission to move the voice into the trusted list. Once approved, a few embeddings are collected and the centroid is saved securely.  Baseline Adaptation:   To reduce false alarms during normal play, streaming statistics (e.g., energy and spectral centroid) are tracked using exponential smoothing or streaming quantile estimators. If the current audio is like the baseline profile, the risk score decreases slightly. These adjustments are conservative, not to suppress the real threat. 18 |   P a g e  3.7 System Implementation Plan  Figure 1.3: High-Level System Architecture  •   Audio Capture:   Continuous recording from the watch mic into a ring buffer. We process in 1-second frames at a 0.5-second hop.  •   Voice Activity Detection:   A tiny VAD module checks for speech or a loud event in frame. If not, it sleeps.  •   Feature Extraction:   Log-Mel spectrogram computation runs locally on device using optimized C++/TFLite.  •   Global Danger Model:   The compacted MobileNet model forecasts   P(distress) .  •   Speaker Verification:   If there is speech, the trust model computes embeddings and compares them to trusted centroids to generate   P(trusted) .  •   Risk Fusion:   Combines probabilities, applies an unknown voice penalty and context- based nudges (like geofence & BLE), then smooths the result over time.  •   Alert Manager:   When risk stays above the threshold for a set duration, it sends an alert via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi to the guardian’s phone. The app displays the alert and optional map location.

19 |   P a g e  •   On-Device Learning:   Maintains embedding buffers and baseline statistics, triggers prompts for adding new trusted voices, and adapts thresholds as needed.  Implementation Tools:  •   Software:  TensorFlow/Keras for model development TensorFlow Lite with XNNPACK delegate for on-device inference WebRTC VAD or Silero VAD Android APIs for audio, geofencing, and BLE scanning PyTorch or Speech Brain for alternative speaker encoders scikit-learn for clustering  •   Hardware:  Wear OS smartwatches (e.g., Snapdragon Wear 4100 or newer) Android smartphone for the   parent device  GPU-enabled development workstation for training and experimentation  3.8   Handling Offline Scenarios and Connectivity Issues.  The solution is tolerant of infrequent internet connections. While offline, all important threat alerts are stored locally on the smartwatch. The alert is time-stamped and queued to be sent to the backend server as soon as the device gets back online to ensure that no alert is lost. To enable a timely response in offline scenarios, the device has a local, attention- seeking audio alarm that can alert individuals in close proximity.
